Hi, D-RUG folks.  Here is an update on how it's been going working with the times and dates in my dataset, along with one more question.

I started out using chron, but (as was predicted) I eventually ended up deciding to switch to POSIXct/lubridate.  (One particular limitation of chron, which became inconvenient for me, is that it cannot be specified as a data class in the colClasses argument of the read.csv function.)

Here is one question that has come up:
Is it possible to use more than one time zone for different items within the same vector of time/date objects?  Here is what I have tried:

> require(lubridate)

Loading required package: lubridate

> my.times <- ymd_hms(c("2012-09-07 12:34:05", NA, "2011-12-30 03:56:02", "2013-01-25 23:13:42"))

 3 parsed with %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S

> my.times

[1] "2012-09-07 12:34:05 UTC" NA                        "2011-12-30 03:56:02 UTC" "2013-01-25 23:13:42 UTC"

> my.times <- force_tz(my.times, "America/Los_Angeles")

> my.times

[1] "2012-09-07 12:34:05 PDT" NA                        "2011-12-30 03:56:02 PST" "2013-01-25 23:13:42 PST"

> tz(my.times[3])

[1] "America/Los_Angeles"

> my.times[3] <- force_tz(my.times[3], "America/Phoenix")

> my.times

[1] "2012-09-07 12:34:05 PDT" NA                        "2011-12-30 02:56:02 PST" "2013-01-25 23:13:42 PST"

> tz(my.times[3])

[1] "America/Los_Angeles"

It looks like it may not be possible to use more than one time zone within the same vector, but if anyone knows of a way, please let me know.

Thanks!

Bonnie

Looks right from what I can tell. It seems to handle the difference in daylight savings time, but it won't store the vector with the various timezones.

my.times <- ymd_hms(c("2012-09-07 12:34:05", NA, "2011-12-30 03:56:02", "2013-01-25 23:13:42"))

Ctown<-force_tz(my.times[3], "America/Chicago")

LA<-force_tz(my.times[1], "America/Los_Angeles")

new.times<-c(Ctown, LA)

new.times #takes into account your local timezone settings (GMT in this case)
#[1] "2011-12-30 06:56:02 GMT" "2012-09-07 20:34:05 BST"

?DateTimeClasses # says the following...
"POSIXct" objects may also have an attribute "tzone", a character vector of length one. If set to a non-empty value, it will determine how the object is converted to class "POSIXlt" and in particular how it is printed. This is usually desirable, but if you want to specify an object in a particular timezone but to be printed in the current timezone you may want to remove the "tzone" attribute (e.g. by c(x)).
#Using c() on "POSIXlt" objects converts them to the current time zone, and on "POSIXct" objects drops any "tzone" attributes (even if they are all marked with the same time zone).

Looks like a POSIXct object can only have a single tz attribute. So a vector can only have one timezone. It looks like, when you vectorize date/time objects, it sets them relative to your local timezone.

If you have a vector of times and a vector of timezones, you can't just put them together.

tzones=c("America/Los_Angeles", "Europe/London")
times<-c("2012-09-07 12:34:05", "2011-12-30 03:56:02")
newest.times<-as.POSIXct(times, tz=tzones)
#Error in strptime(xx, f <- "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS", tz = tz) :
#  invalid 'tz' value

#But... you can do it in a list... A bit of a PITA, but then they're all stored in their correct timezones
df<-data.frame(times, tzones)

#below from https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2004-November/060071.html
list.df<-apply(df, 1, function(x) list(as.POSIXct(x[1], tz=paste(x[2]))))

list.df<-lapply(list.df, "[[", 1)

list.df
#[[1]]
#                    times
#"2012-09-07 12:34:05 PDT"
#
#[[2]]
#                    times
#"2011-12-30 03:56:02 GMT"
#
#Then get your results back out of the list...
as.POSIXct(as.vector(unlist(list.df)), origin="1970-01-01", tz="UTC")
#[1] "2012-09-07 19:34:05 UTC" "2011-12-30 03:56:02 UTC"

I'm not sure if this really helps though. Aren't you simply wanting to compute the time the person slept? and the time difference between when they think they should be up and when they actually get up? If those values are reported in the same timezone?

HTH,

B

For those who reported locations that do not observe DST, I will adjust the time in bed calculations by an hour on the dates with DST transitions to correct them.  And some people did not report a location.  For those people I will exclude the dates with DST transitions from analyses involving time in bed.

Bonnie

messages.body_plain:
Hi D-RUG folks.

I have noticed something odd when using bracket indexing with a logical expression to select a subset of elements, and I am wondering if anyone can explain this behavior.

If there are missing values in a vector, then these seem to be included when selecting a subset this way.

> x <- c(5, NA, 7, 2, 3, NA, 8)
> x
[1]  5 NA  7  2  3 NA  8
> x < 4
[1] FALSE    NA FALSE  TRUE  TRUE    NA FALSE
> x[x < 4]
[1] NA  2  3 NA
> x[x == 3]
[1] NA  3 NA

However, when reassigning the selected subset of elements to a different value, the missing values do not seem to "take" the reassignment.

> x[x < 4] <- 0
> x
[1]  5 NA  7  0  0 NA  8

Is this the expected behavior?  It seems inconsistent.

Thanks.

Bonnie

Hi Bonnie,

This is expected, and a rather nice feature of R — that it truly understands how to handle missing data. Since we don't know the true values of these elements, R will list them (since they *could* be less than four), but doesn't change them (since if they are less than four in the assignment is unknown). It's quite nice, even though the behavior is admittedly a bit strange at first.

Vince

messages.subject: Plotting maps!
messages.body_plain:
These are related to creating figures.

1) I cannot seem to get the border of CA plotted on top of my raster image. I've tried many different packages, and follow directions well, but alas, I'm stuck.

2) I have the same issue with changing the color scheme of the raster rainbow. I'd like to illustrate the spread of occurrence points throughout CA, and use the alt data from worldclim, but I don't want the same color scheme as for the climate data. I think it's confusing to a reader. Preferably, black and white.

Any simple suggestions?

Thanks, Iara

--
Iara Lacher
MESM - Bren School for Environmental Science and Management
PhD Candidate- UC Davis Ecology Graduate Group

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Plotting maps!
messages.body_plain:
Lara,

1) It is probably a projection issue.  What are the projections of the vector (California boundary) and raster layers you are working with?  Have you defined the projection of your raster in your script?  To define the projection of your raster, use projection() from the {raster} package.  If the projections are different I recommend you transform the vector layer to the same as the raster using spTransform() from the {sp} package.

If you provide the projection information, I may be able to give you some more specific suggestions.

Good luck,
Eric
